To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
patients with STEMI presenting to a tertiary care hospital are no more likely to have their reperfusion strategy changed than are those patients presenting to a nontertiariespecialist hospitals.
there is no difference in 1-year mortality, re-infarction, or revascularization rates between STEMI patients treated at tertiary-care versus nontertiary-care hospitals in Canada.
there is no difference in 30-day mortality between patients who receive PCI at tertiary care centres and those who receive PCI at nontertiary centres.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of novel approaches in the management and prevention of heart disease.
the question of whether tertiary-care hospital management of acute myocardial infraction (AMI) patients is really superior to the management of these patients in other settings.
the question of whether the location of the hospital in which a patient is treated affects the quality of the care they receive.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence does not show that patients who are treated at a tertiary care centre for an acute coronary syndrome have better outcomes than patients treated at a nontertiare care centre.
there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the outcomes of patients with STEMI or NSTEMI treated by cardiologists at a tertiary versus a nontertiare hospital are different.
the best outcomes for patients with STEMI are provided in a tertiary care centre.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the quality of care provided to patients with NSTEMI is similar in both the community hospital setting and in tertiary-care centres, with the possible exception of the administration of beta-blockers and aspirin.
the use of PCI is not associated with better outcomes than medical therapy, although the evidence is less robust in this setting.
the best care for the patient is to be found where the patient is.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, despite differences in patient populations, the use of PCI, and the availability of invasive and interventional services, tertiary and nontertiary hospitals are achieving similar clinical outcomes.
the care that you receive at your local hospital is as good as the care that you would receive at a tertiary-care centre, at least in terms of outcomes.
, in the absence of a randomized controlled trial, the best we can do is compare like with like, and we should not be comparing tertiary care with nontertiary settings.
